rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the full elution window and identify critical pairs while limiting the time penalty. The intermediate temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.

Change only gradient duration to test whether the crowded early cluster responds to slope. This establishes whether shallower gradients can resolve the critical pairs before optimizing the elution window and temperature.

The crowded cluster improves with a shallower slope, but the longer run incurs a time penalty. Test higher temperature against injection 1 to seek better selectivity while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.
Test a shallower gradient at the favorable temperature to improve the remaining critical pair. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, leaving room to gain resolution without a time penalty.

The remaining critical pair worsened with a shallower gradient, so slope alone is unlikely to solve it. Raise the starting organic fraction to test selectivity while monitoring retention and separation of the earliest peaks.
Injection 5 reaches the maximum CRF. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method, retaining injection 5 as the benchmark.

Slightly soften the 8-minute gradient by lowering its endpoint, aiming to recover full resolution of both marginal pairs. This slope lies between injections 5 and 6 and should retain a time advantage over injection 5.

Test a higher starting organic fraction to shorten retention and rebalance the two critical early separations. Monitor the earliest peaks for compression, while keeping injection 7 as the fastest fully resolved benchmark.

Test a one-step temperature decrease against injection 7 to measure how the two critical separations trade off. This may reveal a selectivity balance that supports a faster gradient without losing full resolution.

Return to 60 C and trim the gradient endpoint to test a 6-minute program with a slope only slightly steeper than injection 7. This probes whether the marginal pair remains fully resolved while shortening the method.

Injection 10's rounded CRF masks a pair just below full resolution. Lower the endpoint one step to restore separation while retaining the 6-minute gradient, and check whether the last peak still elutes before the gradient ends.

With maximum CRF already secured, test a substantially colder, steeper method for an alternative elution order that could resolve the early cluster faster. The strong endpoint should keep all compounds observable despite increased retention.

Return to 60 C and soften the gradient at the higher starting fraction to recover the early pair that limited injection 8. This tests whether that selectivity region can provide full resolution with a larger margin than injection 7.

The higher starting fraction requires a slower gradient to resolve the early cluster. Return to phi0 0.15 and test a shallower slope for greater resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes; injection 7 remains the fastest fully resolved benchmark.

Preserve injection 7's initial gradient slope but end the ramp earlier, testing whether a short final hold can retain maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient. The last compound will likely elute during the hold, so its retention time will determine whether this is useful.

Test the unexamined starting fraction between 0.05 and 0.15 with a relatively steep gradient to map the early-cluster selectivity tradeoff. Injection 7 remains the fastest method with every pair confirmed above R = 1.5.
Back off one endpoint step from the fastest fully resolved method to increase the critical pair's resolution margin. This should retain maximum CRF with only a modest increase in last-peak time.

Test whether a shallower gradient can increase the minimum resolution while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes and preserving maximum CRF. Injection 7 remains the preferred speed benchmark; this run explores a more forgiving alternative.

Compare directly with injection 18 to test whether the higher starting fraction balances the critical early separations while shortening retention. The shallower slope should help recover the pair that limited injection 8, with maximum CRF already secured.

Raise the endpoint one grid step from injection 7 to test the remaining speed boundary between its full resolution and injection 6's slight losses. Retain injection 7 if either critical pair drops below R = 1.5.

The faster endpoint in injection 20 lost full resolution, so retain injection 7 as the speed benchmark. Test this intermediate slope for more separation margin than injection 17 with less retention than injection 14, while preserving maximum CRF.

Test whether injection 19's larger separation margin for the later member of the early cluster permits operation at 55 C while retaining maximum CRF. This evaluates a lower-temperature alternative; injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Return to 60 C and steepen injection 19's gradient modestly to reduce retention while targeting full resolution. Its slope remains slightly shallower than injection 13's successful slope, so maximum CRF should be preserved.

Preserve injection 21's successful slope while shortening the programmed gradient to 6 minutes. The critical early separations should remain unchanged; check whether the final hold keeps the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes and preserves maximum CRF.

Use the final injection to test an intermediate slope between injections 14 and 21, targeting maximum CRF with additional resolution margin and a last peak below 10 minutes. Injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.
